🟡 ReVillage Green Valley

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website

ReVillage Green Valley is a place-rooted initiative reweaving community through land-based regeneration and collective care, responding to wildfires, housing displacement, ecological degradation, and social isolation.

Bioregional Context

Green Valley exists within West Sonoma County, California, centered around the town of Graton with approximately 1,800 residents. The bioregion is defined by rolling hills, vineyards, farmland, and forests, with the Green Valley watershed serving as a natural boundary.

Background


The Green Valley watershed is a compact 40-square-mile bioregion in western Sonoma County, California, centered on Graton (about 1,800 residents). Rolling hills, vineyards, farmland, and forests define the area, with the watershed itself as a natural frame. Over the past century the local economy moved from apples toward wine; the community is now writing another chapter.

Origins and Network


ReVillage Green Valley grew out of grassroots organizing. They describe themselves as accidental bioregional organizers—the work began with love of place and gathering alongside neighbors who had long stewarded the land.

They envision a local economy grounded in ecology, equity, and cultural renewal, co-created with First Nations peoples, Latino farmworkers, Zen communities, and other long-term residents. Wildfires, housing pressure, ecological decline, and isolation are the overlapping crises; their response is to reweave community through land-based regeneration and shared care.

Activities

🔸

Green Valley Commons

In year one they formed a nonprofit and turned a former gas station at the town center into a new town square—Green Valley Commons. They raised over $1 million through land-trust funding, public sources, private gifts, and crowdfunding, then ran a community design process so neighbors could imagine the shared space. The Commons now hosts cooperative workdays, events, youth gatherings, and early shared childcare and food-growing. A lease-to-own agreement gives site control; they are working toward an outright purchase. Early support is in place; they seek $250,000 in catalytic capital to secure title, advance priority capital work (permitting, kitchen, ADA access), and strengthen programming and local governance.

🔸

Arts & Museum of the Future

On site they developed a “Museum of the Future”: archives and time capsules honor seven generations back; school visits and participatory visioning imagine seven generations forward—a place where past and future meet in the present and stories of land and people can be held while new possibilities are shaped together. Community councils—arts, design-build, elders—guide decisions through town halls and co-design. A seasonal rhythm of festivals, monthly work parties, potlucks, and resilience trainings teaches mutual aid in crises such as immigration raids or natural disasters.

🔸

Community Land Trust Formation

The team is forming a community land trust to hold the Green Valley Commons in perpetuity for collective well-being. The trust is meant to anchor cooperative housing and ecological stewardship, limit speculation, and encode equitable access and multigenerational ownership. The effort is early: governance protocols, counsel from land-justice allies, and legal design to match values. Long term, they picture affordable housing, cooperative enterprise space, a community kitchen, and commons governance—all held through the trust.

🔸

ReVillage Co-Op Enterprises

They are breaking ground on a community-owned enterprise—a public house, marketplace, café, food hub, and small-business incubator—in a long-vacant historic firehouse (once a train station) facing the new town square. The Community Food Hub & Marketplace is underway; a Community Farm Project is funded and launching soon. Each effort is co-created with communities already in place, toward a future in right relationship with land and history. Smaller cooperatives are forming in the ReVillage ecosystem: an intergenerational childcare collective, a local food and land-care initiative, and service ventures emerging through relationships. They are testing income-sharing, cooperative ownership, and regenerative service models that can sustain livelihoods where centralized systems often overlook rural communities. Technical help on legal structure and seed funding for place-rooted enterprises remain needs—the building blocks of a local economy that can support people while regenerating land.

🔸

Local Governance Innovation

They partnered with the Graton Community Services District (sewer) to broaden its mandate toward parks, recreation, and eventually ecosystem services and recommoning. The district now holds the town square and additional public space, with more planned. They also work with the Gold Ridge Resource Conservation District—linking formal institutions to an informal web of residents, businesses, and volunteers.

🔸

ReVillaging Toolkit and Learning Exchange

ReVillage wants to help other places adapt this model. They are co-developing a “ReVillaging Toolkit”—legal templates, governance patterns, land strategies, and narrative resources. A hosted residency at Green Valley Commons is planned so practitioners can immerse in the work and learn peer-to-peer. They hope for a wider network of village-builders across California and the Pacific Coast to share resources, iterate together, and spread the cultural shift the work implies.

Vision and Legacy


They are watching how commons, shared culture, and a regenerative economy might braid over time, and welcome partners who want to prototype village-scale regeneration built for interdependence, cultural vitality, and ecological repair.

By strengthening intergenerational, locally governed systems, they aim to offer a replicable model of “revillaging” for rural and peri-urban landscapes. The same crises—fire, displacement, ecological harm, isolation—are addressed by reweaving community through land-based regeneration and collective care.

In the Green Valley watershed—hills, vineyards, farmland, forest—people are practicing interdependence with one another, with nonhuman nature, and with the living Earth: one gas station, one firehouse, one enterprise at a time, starting from love of place and neighbors who show up to care.
